title: Playing soft: dynamics in the old New Orleans bands
summary: The triple-forte tradition Jelly described, Bolden's remark about hearing dancers drag their feet, and the quiet chorus before the end.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I came across the old notes I'd taken once over at Preservation Hall about five or six years ago, or maybe ten years ago, I think they were. I happened to be sitting out in the carriageway there on those benches, and Jim was there. He wasn't playing that night. And so I copied down the remarks he was making after he left. I didn't copy them down, but mostly word for word. And he would say, what kind of a band, what kind of a trumpet player? Where's the trumpet player? He'd keep saying, where's the trumpet player? Don't hear the trumpet player. You know, he couldn't see in there. He knew that he wasn't playing. He was just ridiculing him. And he'd say, that's no way to have a band. That's no way for a trumpet player to do to put his horn down at all, you see. So in some cases, you might think that would add more monotony to the music, you know, everything the same. But another thing they did in the old days, which Jelly talks about a lot, the triple 40 bands, as Jelly calls them, that they should, you know, this business of the glass of water. He goes into that on one of the Library of Congress, where if you have a glass of water half full, you can add to it and take away and all. In the old days, they had these routines Bunkies talked about and Baby Dodds used to talk about it too. Most of the New Orleans bands would follow. It was almost a convention, you might say, a tradition to do it that way, that you hit the introduction loud, as they say, the forte, and then maybe they'd drop down just a little bit, but still with the full tone for the first few choruses, and then they'd drop down quite soft, maybe come up a little bit, and right before the end, they'd drop down so soft that you could hardly hear it. There was somebody who was, when I was down in Bermuda a month ago, must have been Willie Humphrey or Percy or somebody talking about, too, how some of the dances they used to play, they'd play so soft too, that you couldn't, they couldn't hear themselves play, and that next to the last chorus or so.
I think it was King Oliver who said that he wanted his band to be able to play so soft they could hear the dancers shuffling.

Yeah, I think that's quoted in Jasmine as a Bolden remark, whether it was, yeah, it was supposed to be a Bolden remark. They say, way down, way down low, so I can hear those whores drag their feet on the floor. I don't know who told me that, Richard M. Jones or somebody, that they'd heard Bolden say that. I don't know whether it's strictly true, but anyway, that was very much the New Orleans tradition. The Ori band followed that.
What was that? Was that for the, part of the form of it, the definite form, or did it build momentum towards the end, or?

Well, yeah, just to give more contrast, and then to make the final all-out chorus, as they called it, more effective. More effective, yeah. I know once, I used to question Minnetta, since he played violin, whether you could really hear the violin in the band, because you'd wonder, you know, since I try to play violin myself, in, say, a ragtime band, and half the time you can't hear it unless there's a microphone and amplifier there, and Minnetta said, too, you could hardly hear the violin most of the time. Maybe sometime, the only time you'd hear it would be that very soft chorus before the end. That's maybe also the only time you'd really hear the guitar come out good, too, because they used guitar in the old-time bands rather than the banjo before, say, the 1920s. The banjo.
